--- title: "Tutorial: Using the emmeans R Package" date: "1/6/2025" date-modified: last-modified date-format: long --- ## 1. Introduction The `emmeans` package in R simplifies post-hoc analysis and estimation of marginal means from statistical models. It provides tools to estimate, compare, and test means across levels of predictors while accounting for the model structure. ## Overview - **Purpose**: Provides estimated marginal means (EMMs) or least-squares means. - **Core Features**: - Compute EMMs for any combination of factors. - Perform pairwise comparisons or custom contrasts. - Integrate with popular visualization packages like `ggplot2`. - Easily handle model interactions and transformations. - **Key Supported Models**: - Linear models (`lm`, `aov`). - Generalized linear models (`glm`). - Mixed-effects models (`lme4`, `nlme`). ## What Are Marginal Means? Marginal means are predicted values from a model, adjusted to account for the distribution of covariates or other factors. They provide a clearer interpretation of group effects compared to raw means. ## 2. Getting Started ## Loading the Package ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(emmeans) ``` ::: ## Example Dataset We will use the `warpbreaks` dataset, which contains data on the number of breaks in yarn (response variable `breaks`) across two factors: wool type (`wool`) and tension level (`tension`). ## Basic Model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fitting a linear model lm_model <- lm(breaks ~ wool * tension, data = warpbreaks) ``` ::: ## Basic Marginal Means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Marginal means by wool emmeans(lm_model, ~ wool) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL A 31.0 2.11 48 26.8 35.3 B 25.3 2.11 48 21.0 29.5 Results are averaged over the levels of: tension Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ## 3. Key Functions in `emmeans` ## 3.1 `emmeans()` The `emmeans()` function is the foundation of the package, used to estimate marginal means. **Usage**: ```r emmeans(object, specs, by = NULL, options = NULL, ...) ``` **Arguments**: - **`object`**: A fitted model (e.g., `lm`, `glm`, or `lmer`). - **`specs`**: Formula specifying factors for which marginal means are computed. Use `|` to specify conditions (e.g., `~ wool | tension`). - **`by`**: Variables to group results. - **`options`**: Adjustments like type of prediction (`response`, `link`, etc.). **Examples**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Marginal means for wool emmeans(lm_model, ~wool) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL A 31.0 2.11 48 26.8 35.3 B 25.3 2.11 48 21.0 29.5 Results are averaged over the levels of: tension Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Marginal means of tension within each wool group emmeans(lm_model, ~ tension | wool) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: tension emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL L 44.6 3.65 48 37.2 51.9 M 24.0 3.65 48 16.7 31.3 H 24.6 3.65 48 17.2 31.9 wool = B: tension emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL L 28.2 3.65 48 20.9 35.6 M 28.8 3.65 48 21.4 36.1 H 18.8 3.65 48 11.4 26.1 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ## 3.2 `contrast()` The `contrast()` function performs post-hoc comparisons between marginal means, such as pairwise comparisons or custom contrasts. **Usage**: ```r contrast(object, method = "pairwise", interaction = FALSE, by = NULL, ...) ``` **Arguments**: - **`object`**: An `emmGrid` object (output of `emmeans()`). - **`method`**: Type of comparison. Common methods: - `"pairwise"`: Pairwise differences. - `"poly"`: Polynomial contrasts. - `"eff"`: Effect contrasts (deviation from overall mean). - **`interaction`**: Defines interaction contrasts, generating contrasts of contrasts for multi-factor interactions. - **`by`**: Grouping variables for separate contrasts. **Examples**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pairwise comparisons of tension levels warp.emm <- emmeans(lm_model, ~ tension | wool) contrast(warp.emm, method = "pairwise") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M 20.556 5.16 48 3.986 0.0007 L - H 20.000 5.16 48 3.878 0.0009 M - H -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9936 wool = B: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9936 L - H 9.444 5.16 48 1.831 0.1704 M - H 10.000 5.16 48 1.939 0.1389 P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Custom contrasts for tension levels contrast(warp.emm, list(mid.vs.ends = c(-1, 2, -1) / 2, lo.vs.hi = c(1, 0, -1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value mid.vs.ends -10.56 4.47 48 -2.363 0.0222 lo.vs.hi 20.00 5.16 48 3.878 0.0003 wool = B: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value mid.vs.ends 5.28 4.47 48 1.182 0.2432 lo.vs.hi 9.44 5.16 48 1.831 0.0733 ``` ::: ::: ## 3.3 `pairs()` This function simplifies pairwise comparisons (shortcut for `contrast(…, method = "pairwise")`). **Usage**: ```r pairs(object, reverse = FALSE, ...) ``` **Arguments**: - **`reverse`**: If `TRUE`, reverses the order of comparisons. **Example**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pairwise comparisons for tension pairs(warp.emm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M 20.556 5.16 48 3.986 0.0007 L - H 20.000 5.16 48 3.878 0.0009 M - H -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9936 wool = B: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9936 L - H 9.444 5.16 48 1.831 0.1704 M - H 10.000 5.16 48 1.939 0.1389 P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates ``` ::: ::: ## 4. Advanced Functionality ## 4.1 Interaction Contrasts Interaction contrasts allow you to compare interactions between factors. The `interaction` argument in `contrast()` enables this. **Example**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Interaction contrast for wool and tension interaction_contrast <- contrast(warp.emm, interaction = c(wool = "eff", tension = "poly")) interaction_contrast ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: tension_eff estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L effect 13.52 2.98 48 4.540 <.0001 M effect -7.04 2.98 48 -2.363 0.0222 H effect -6.48 2.98 48 -2.177 0.0344 wool = B: tension_eff estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L effect 2.96 2.98 48 0.995 0.3247 M effect 3.52 2.98 48 1.182 0.2432 H effect -6.48 2.98 48 -2.177 0.0344 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coef(interaction_contrast) # View coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|tension |wool | c.1| c.2| c.3| c.4| c.5| c.6| |:-------|:----|----------:|----------:|----------:|----------:|----------:|----------:| |L |A | 0.6666667| -0.3333333| -0.3333333| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| |M |A | -0.3333333| 0.6666667| -0.3333333| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| |H |A | -0.3333333| -0.3333333| 0.6666667| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| |L |B | 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.6666667| -0.3333333| -0.3333333| |M |B | 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| -0.3333333| 0.6666667| -0.3333333| |H |B | 0.0000000| 0.0000000| 0.0000000| -0.3333333| -0.3333333| 0.6666667|
::: ::: ## 4.2 Scaling and Offsetting Use `scale` and `offset` to transform results for interpretation (e.g., converting units). **Example**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Convert temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit mod <- lm(Water.Temp ~ poly(stack.loss, degree = 2), data = stackloss) emm <- emmeans(mod, "stack.loss", at = list(stack.loss = 10 * (1:4))) contrast(emm, "identity", scale = 9 / 5, offset = 32) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value stack.loss10 65.9 0.833 18 79.138 <.0001 stack.loss20 72.1 1.020 18 71.059 <.0001 stack.loss30 76.8 1.160 18 66.067 <.0001 stack.loss40 80.0 1.720 18 46.389 <.0001 ``` ::: ::: ## 4.3 Adjusting for Multiple Comparisons Use the `adjust` argument to control corrections like Bonferroni or Tukey: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrast(warp.emm, method = "pairwise", adjust = "tukey") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M 20.556 5.16 48 3.986 0.0007 L - H 20.000 5.16 48 3.878 0.0009 M - H -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9936 wool = B: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9936 L - H 9.444 5.16 48 1.831 0.1704 M - H 10.000 5.16 48 1.939 0.1389 P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates ``` ::: ::: ## 5. Visualizing Results ## Interaction Plots The `emmip()` function creates interaction plots to visualize EMMs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Interaction plot for wool and tension library(ggplot2) emmip(warp.emm, wool ~ tension) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Pairwise Comparisons Plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pairwise comparison plot plot(pairs(warp.emm)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 6. Common Issues and Troubleshooting ## Common Issues 1. **Degrees of freedom not available**: - Some models (e.g., Bayesian) require manual specification of degrees of freedom. 2. **Invalid contrast method**: - Ensure the `method` matches the structure of your `emmGrid` object. ## Best Practices - Always inspect the `emmGrid` object using `summary()` before applying contrasts. - Use `confint()` to obtain confidence intervals. - Apply `adjust` for proper corrections in multiple comparisons. ## 7. Detailed Argument Reference ## `emmeans()` Specific Arguments - **`specs`**: Defines the terms of interest. For example: - `~ factor1`: Marginal means for `factor1`. - `~ factor1 | factor2`: Marginal means of `factor1` grouped by `factor2`. ## `contrast()` Specific Arguments - **`interaction`**: Defines contrasts for interactions. Example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrast(warp.emm, interaction = list(wool = "pairwise", tension = "eff")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: tension_pairwise estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M 20.556 5.16 48 3.986 0.0002 L - H 20.000 5.16 48 3.878 0.0003 M - H -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9147 wool = B: tension_pairwise estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L - M -0.556 5.16 48 -0.108 0.9147 L - H 9.444 5.16 48 1.831 0.0733 M - H 10.000 5.16 48 1.939 0.0584 ``` ::: ::: - **`scale` and `offset`**: For transforming estimates. Example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrast(warp.emm, method = "identity", scale = 2, offset = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wool = A: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L 90.1 7.29 48 12.355 <.0001 M 49.0 7.29 48 6.718 <.0001 H 50.1 7.29 48 6.871 <.0001 wool = B: contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value L 57.4 7.29 48 7.876 <.0001 M 58.6 7.29 48 8.028 <.0001 H 38.6 7.29 48 5.286 <.0001 ``` ::: ::: ## 8. Conclusion The `emmeans` package provides a robust framework for estimating and interpreting marginal means. With extensive support for complex models and versatile post-hoc analysis tools, it is essential for data analysis workflows. ## Next Steps - Explore advanced vignettes in the package documentation. - Integrate results into visualizations with `ggplot2`. ## 9. References and Resources - [emmeans CRAN Page](https://cran.r-project.org/package=emmeans) - [Vignettes: Estimated Marginal Means](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/emmeans/vignettes/emmeans.html) - [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/rvlenth/emmeans)
